references.text: Job says that God humbles the proud but saves the humble: 'For he humiliates the proud, but saves those who cast down their eyes' (Job 22:29). This directly mirrors the principle Jesus states: whoever humbles themselves will be exalted.
Proverbs teaches: 'Pride leads to disgrace, but with humility comes honor' (Proverbs 29:23). This is the same principle Jesus expresses in his concluding statement.
'He mocks mockers but gives grace to the humble' (Proverbs 3:34). The tax collector who humbled himself received grace (was justified), while the Pharisee who exalted himself remained without grace.

Ezekiel conveys God's word about bringing down what is high and lifting up what is low: 'The high will be brought low, and the low will be raised high' (Ezekiel 21:31). The same principle of reversal that Jesus expresses.
God dwells with those who are crushed and humble in spirit, to give life to the humble's spirit (Isaiah 57:15). The tax collector with his humble prayer is an illustration of this.

'A broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise' (Psalm 51:19). The tax collector's prayer—'God, be merciful to me, a sinner'—is precisely the expression of a broken and contrite heart that God accepts.
Jesus repeats exactly the same principle: 'Whoever exalts themselves will be humbled, and whoever humbles themselves will be exalted' (Matthew 23:12). A parallel statement in another context.

Also in the parable about seats at the table, Jesus states the same: 'For everyone who exalts themselves will be humbled, and whoever humbles themselves will be exalted' (Luke 14:11). A close parallel in both wording and theme.
James quotes Proverbs and writes: 'God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble' (James 4:6). The Pharisee represents the proud, the tax collector the humble.
'Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you' (James 4:10). A direct New Testament parallel to Jesus' words that whoever humbles themselves will be exalted.

Peter urges: 'Clothe yourselves with humility toward one another! For God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble. Humble yourselves therefore under God's mighty hand, so that he may exalt you in his time' (1 Peter 5:5-6). The same principle of humility and exaltation.
Paul writes that people 'are justified freely by his grace' (Romans 3:24). The tax collector went home justified—not because of any merit of his own, but because he cast himself upon God's grace.
